title: Virtual Lists and Performance at Scale

subChunks.title: Virtual Lists and Performance at Scale
subChunks.hookHtml: Rendering 10,000 items in a list is slow not because React is slow — it's because mounting 10,000 DOM nodes is slow. Virtualisation solves this by only rendering the items currently visible in the viewport. This lesson covers windowing/virtualisation with TanStack Virtual, bundle analysis, and the performance investigation workflow for large React applications.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The problem: too many DOM nodes

A list of 10,000 items creates 10,000 DOM nodes. Even if they're offscreen, the browser tracks them in the layout tree. Initial render takes 2+ seconds. Scroll is janky. The fix: only render the ~20 items visible in the viewport.

TanStack Virtual — virtualise any list or grid

import { useVirtualizer } from '@tanstack/react-virtual';
import { useRef } from 'react';

function VirtualQuestList({ quests }) {
  const parentRef = useRef(null);

  const virtualiser = useVirtualizer({
    count: quests.length,
    getScrollElement: () => parentRef.current,
    estimateSize: () => 50, // Estimated item height in px
  });

  return (
    // Scrollable container — fixed height required:
    <div
      ref={parentRef}
      style={{ height: '600px', overflow: 'auto' }}
    >
      {/* Inner div has the total height — creates the scrollbar: */}
      <div style={{ height: `${virtualiser.getTotalSize()}px`, position: 'relative' }}>
        {virtualiser.getVirtualItems().map(virtualItem => (
          <div
            key={virtualItem.key}
            style={{
              position: 'absolute',
              top: 0,
              transform: `translateY(${virtualItem.start}px)`,
              width: '100%',
              height: `${virtualItem.size}px`,
            }}
          >
            {/* Only this item renders — not all 10,000: */}
            <QuestItem quest={quests[virtualItem.index]} />
          </div>
        ))}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

Bundle analysis — finding what's bloating your app

# With Vite:
npm run build -- --report
# Opens bundle visualiser

# With Webpack:
npx webpack-bundle-analyzer stats.json

# Quick check with source-map-explorer:
npx source-map-explorer 'build/static/js/*.js'

Common bundle bloat sources:

  • date-fns imported as import * from 'date-fns' instead of import { format } from 'date-fns'
  • lodash imported as import _ from 'lodash' — use lodash-es or per-method imports
  • A charting library (recharts, chart.js) loaded on every page instead of code-split
  • Duplicate dependencies from nested node_modules

The performance investigation workflow

  1. Lighthouse CI: catch regressions in CI before they reach production
  2. React DevTools Profiler: identify which components render most
  3. Chrome Performance tab: long tasks, layout thrash, paint times
  4. Bundle analyser: what's in the initial bundle that shouldn't be
  5. Network tab: asset sizes, waterfall, cache headers

Vex: "The single highest-impact React performance intervention is usually not adding memo or useCallback — it's removing a 200kb library you forgot about from the initial bundle. Profile, then investigate. The bottleneck is almost never where you expect."

Code splitting strategies

// Route-level splitting (most impactful):
const Dashboard = lazy(() => import('./pages/Dashboard'));
const Analytics = lazy(() => import('./pages/Analytics'));

// Component-level splitting for heavy widgets:
const ChartWidget = lazy(() => import('./components/ChartWidget'));

// Library splitting — load heavy library only when needed:
const loadPDFGenerator = () => import('pdfmake/build/pdfmake');

storyBeats.text: The quest board renders 10,000 entries. Initial load: 4.2 seconds. Scroll: 12fps. The React DevTools Profiler shows 8,000 mounted components. Vex opens the virtualisation docs.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The browser mounts every item in the DOM — even the 9,980 that are offscreen. Virtualisation only mounts what's visible. The inner div maintains the correct total height for the scrollbar. Only 20 items exist in the DOM at any time. The rest are created and destroyed as the user scrolls.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: After virtualisation, open the bundle analyser. Look for the hidden 200kb date library you import one function from. Look for the chart component included in the initial bundle for a page 5% of users visit. Bundle size is usually a bigger win than component memoisation.

storyBeats.speaker: Virtualised list — only visible items mount

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a virtualised list of 10,000 items:

  • Generate an array of 10,000 quest objects with id and title
  • Use useVirtualizer from @tanstack/react-virtual to render only the visible items
  • The scrollable container must have a fixed height (use 500px)
  • Each item should have data-testid="virtual-item"
  • Show the total count: data-testid="total-count"
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a virtualised data grid (not a list — 2D) using TanStack Virtual with both row and column virtualisation. The grid should handle 10,000 rows × 20 columns. Each cell shows its row/column index. Use useVirtualizer for both dimensions. Add sorting on column header click (sort only the visible window, not all 10,000 rows). Profile the render time with and without virtualisation using the <Profiler> component.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the problem that virtualisation solves — why does rendering 10,000 list items hurt performance even if they're off-screen? Walk through how TanStack Virtual works: what does the outer container do, what does the inner div's height do, and why are positions absolute rather than relative? Then explain what bundle analysis reveals and what the most common sources of bundle bloat are.

questions.prompt: Why does a list of 10,000 items hurt performance even if most items are offscreen?
options: All 10,000 DOM nodes exist in the browser's layout tree — they take time to mount, consume memory, and cause layout calculations even when invisible
React re-renders all 10,000 items on every parent state change
Offscreen items trigger scroll event listeners
The browser downloads images for all 10,000 items eagerly
questions.answer: All 10,000 DOM nodes exist in the browser's layout tree — they take time to mount, consume memory, and cause layout calculations even when invisible
questions.explanation: Every DOM node has a cost regardless of visibility: initial creation time, memory for the node object and its styles, inclusion in layout calculations. 10,000 nodes at ~1ms each = 10 seconds to mount. Virtualisation limits the DOM to ~20 nodes at a time — creation is instant, memory is minimal, and layout calculations are trivial.

questions.prompt: In a virtualised list, why does the inner container div need `height: totalSize` and items need `position: absolute`?
options: The inner height creates the correct scrollbar size without all items present; absolute positioning places each item at its exact scroll offset so layout is correct
The height is needed for CSS grid to work; absolute positioning avoids float issues
The inner height prevents layout shift; absolute positioning enables GPU acceleration
These are required by the browser's virtual scroll API
questions.answer: The inner height creates the correct scrollbar size without all items present; absolute positioning places each item at its exact scroll offset so layout is correct
questions.explanation: If only 20 items exist in the DOM, the scrollbar would only be tall enough for 20 items. Setting the inner div's height to totalItems × itemHeight gives the correct scrollbar size. Items are positioned absolutely at their calculated scroll offset (item index × item height) so they appear in the right place as the user scrolls.

questions.prompt: Your bundle analyser shows that `lodash` is 71kb of your 80kb initial bundle. What is the correct fix?
options: Import only the specific functions you use (`import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'`) or switch to lodash-es with tree-shaking
Upgrade to the latest version of lodash which has a smaller bundle size
Move lodash imports into a useEffect so they load lazily
Add lodash to the Webpack externals config
questions.answer: Import only the specific functions you use (`import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'`) or switch to lodash-es with tree-shaking
questions.explanation: import _ from 'lodash' imports the entire library. import debounce from 'lodash/debounce' imports only the debounce module (~2kb). Alternatively, switching to lodash-es (the ES modules version) enables tree-shaking — your bundler can drop all unused functions. The same principle applies to date-fns, rxjs, and other large utility libraries.

questions.prompt: What should you do FIRST when investigating a slow React application?
options: Open the React DevTools Profiler and record the slow interaction — find which components render, how often, and for how long
Enable production mode and measure again
Add useCallback to every event handler
questions.answer: Open the React DevTools Profiler and record the slow interaction — find which components render, how often, and for how long
questions.explanation: Premature optimisation is adding memo/useCallback/useMemo without evidence. The Profiler gives you evidence: which component renders in 200ms, which renders 500 times per second, which is the actual bottleneck. After profiling, you might discover the problem is a 500kb image, a synchronous localStorage read, or a missing virtualisation — not anything useMemo would fix.
